MergeSort and comparisons (4%)

Consider the following input to MergeSort, implemented as in CLRS Section 2.3.

How many comparisons between two elements does MergeSort make in total on this input? Comparisons with \(\infty\) in Merge are not counted.

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: MergeSort and comparisons (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: The two recursive calls on the lists \(\langle 4,3\rangle\) and \(\langle 1,2\rangle\) each use one comparison. After these calls, the sorted lists \(\langle 3,4\rangle\) and \(\langle 1,2\rangle\) are merged. This merge uses two comparisons: \(3\) against \(1\) and then \(3\) against \(2\). In total, \(1+1+2=4\) comparisons are therefore used.

data.stimulus:
Asymptotic bounds (4%)

Which of the running times below are \(O(n^2)\)?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Asymptotic bounds (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: We check whether each function grows at most quadratically. \(2^{\lg n} = n\), since \(\lg n = \log_2 n\), and therefore \(2^{\lg n} = n\). Hence the function is also \(O(n^2)\). In contrast, \(n^3\) grows faster than \(n^2\) and is therefore not \(O(n^2)\). \(1.5^{n}\) grows faster than any polynomial in \(n\), including \(n^2\), and is therefore not \(O(n^2)\). Finally, \(\sqrt{n} = n^{1/2}\) and \(\log n\) both grow asymptotically slower than \(n^2\), so they are \(O(n^2)\).

data.stimulus:
Solving recurrences (4%)

Assume that \(n\) is a power of 2, that \(T_i(1)=1\) for \(i=1,\dots,6\), and consider the recurrences below. Which of the following statements are true?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Solving recurrences (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale:
The master theorem can be used to find a solution to all of the recurrences: Write \(T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n)\) and compare \(f(n)\) with \(n^{\log_b a}\).

  1. \(a=2,b=2\): \(n^{\log_b a}=n\), and \(f(n)=n\log n=\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log n)\), so \(T_1(n)=\Theta(n\log^2 n)\) (the statement is false).
  2. \(a=4,b=4\): \(n^{\log_b a}=n\), and \(f(n)=n^2=\Omega(n^{1+\varepsilon})\) with the regularity condition \(af(n/b)=4(n/4)^2=n^2/4\le c n^2\), so \(T_2(n)=\Theta(n^2)\) (true).
  3. \(a=4,b=2\): \(n^{\log_b a}=n^2\), and \(f(n)=n=O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\), so \(T_3(n)=\Theta(n^2)\) (true).
  4. \(a=4,b=2\): \(n^{\log_b a}=n^2\), and \(f(n)=n^2=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})\), so \(T_4(n)=\Theta(n^2\log n)\) (false).
  5. \(a=8,b=2\): \(n^{\log_b a}=n^3\), and \(f(n)=n^2 \log n = O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\), so \(T_5(n)=\Theta(n^3)\) (true).
  6. \(a=8,b=2\): \(n^{\log_b a}=n^3\), and \(f(n)=n^3=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})\), so \(T_6(n)=\Theta(n^3\log n)\) (false).

data.stimulus:
Setting up a recurrence (4%)

Consider the following recursive algorithm:

Assume that \(n\) is a power of 2 and that all elementary operations take constant time. Which recurrence best describes the running time \(T(n)\) of the following call? \[\text{RecursiveMystery}(A,1,n)\]

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Setting up a recurrence (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: For \(n>1\) the algorithm makes two recursive calls, and each call works on one half of the array, with input size \(n/2\). This contributes \(2T(n/2)\). After the recursive calls, the two nested loops count the number of pairs of equal elements where one element lies in the left half and the other in the right half. There are \((n/2)\cdot(n/2)=\Theta(n^2)\) such pairs, and the test and any increment take constant time for each pair. The running time is therefore described by \[T(n)=2T(n/2)+\Theta(n^2),\] with base case \(T(1)=\Theta(1)\).

Consider the following algorithm, which takes a positive integer \(n\) as input:

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Running time analysis (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: The outermost forloop runs \(n\) times. The next forloop runs \(i\) times, so the total number of pairs \((i,j)\) is \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \Theta(n^2)\). For each such pair, \(k\) is quadrupled in each iteration of the whileloop, so it runs \(\Theta(\log n)\) times. Hence the total running time is \(\Theta(n^2 \log n)\).

data.stimulus:
Dynamic tables (4%)

We consider dynamic tables as described in CLRS Section 16.4.2 (the version with both Table-Insert and Table-Delete). An empty table \(T\) is initialized with \[T.num = 0,\qquad T.size = 0.\]

Then the following operations are performed in order: Insert, Insert, Insert, Insert, Insert, Delete, Delete, Delete, Delete, Insert, Insert, Insert. Which of the following statements are true after the last operation?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Dynamic tables (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale:
After the first five insertions we have \[(T.num,T.size)=(5,8).\]

After three deletions the state is \((2,8)\), and the load factor is exactly \(1/4\), so the table is not halved (yet). After the fourth deletion the intermediate state becomes \((1,8)\), where the load factor is strictly less than \(1/4\), and the table is therefore halved to size 4: \[(5,8)\rightarrow(4,8)\rightarrow(3,8)\rightarrow(2,8)\rightarrow(1,8)\rightarrow(1,4).\]

The last three insertions give \[(1,4)\rightarrow(2,4)\rightarrow(3,4)\rightarrow(4,4).\] None of these triggers a doubling, so the final state is \(T.num=4, T.size=4\).

data.stimulus:
Fibonacci heaps (4%)

In Fibonacci heaps (cf. CLRS online Chapter 19) the potential function is given by \[\Phi(H)=t(H)+2\,m(H),\] where \(t(H)\) is the number of nodes in the root list and \(m(H)\) is the number of marked nodes. Suppose we have a Fibonacci heap \(H\) with minimum value 10 (i.e., Minimum\((H)\) returns the key with value 10). Let \(x\) be a key in \(H\) with value \(87\). Which of the following operations on \(H\) will always cause the potential function to increase (based on the stated properties)?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Fibonacci heaps (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale:
A Minimum operation does not change the heap; it only returns a pointer to the minimum node. Therefore neither \(t(H)\) nor \(m(H)\) changes, and the potential does not increase.

A Fib-Heap-Decrease-Key operation increases the potential only in some cases. For example, if \(x\) is already a root, or if the new key 42 still does not violate the heap order with respect to \(x\)'s parent, no cut is performed and \(t(H)\) and \(m(H)\) are unchanged.

A Fib-Heap-Delete operation is performed by first decreasing the key to \(-\infty\) with Fib-Heap-Decrease-Key and then performing Fib-Heap-Extract-Min. The Decrease-Key step can mark a node (through a cascading cut), but Extract-Min does not mark nodes; instead it can remove roots while consolidating the root list (and unmark nodes when they are linked). Therefore there is no guaranteed increase in \(\Phi(H)\).

A Fib-Heap-Insert operation always inserts the new node as an unmarked root in the root list. Hence \(t(H)\) increases by 1, while \(m(H)\) is unchanged, regardless of the value of the new key.

Red-black invariants (4%)

Which of the following statements always hold for red-black search trees (are invariants or consequences of invariants)?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Red-black invariants (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: Statements 2, 4, 6, 7, 8 are exactly the five classic red-black properties: nodes are colored red/black, the root is black, NIL leaves are black, red nodes have black children, and all paths from a node to a leaf have the same number of black nodes (the same black-height). Statement 3 about the height is a consequence of the classic invariants, and is therefore also a valid invariant in itself. The two structural statements about the number of children do not hold in general.

data.stimulus:
Shortest paths (4%)

Consider the following weighted, directed graph:

Suppose Dijkstra's algorithm is run with source vertex a. In which order are the vertices extracted from the priority queue?

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Shortest paths (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: From the source vertex a we first get the distances \(d[b]=4\) and \(d[c]=2\). Therefore c is extracted next. The edge \((\mathbf{c},\mathbf{b})\) improves the distance to b to \(3\), so b is extracted before the remaining vertices. Next, the edge \((\mathbf{b},\mathbf{d})\) improves the distance to d to \(6\), while e has distance \(8\) via c. Therefore d is extracted before e. The edge \((\mathbf{d},\mathbf{f})\) gives \(d[f]=7\), so f is extracted before e. The order is therefore a, c, b, d, f, e.

data.stimulus:
Parallel algorithms (4%)

Suppose that a parallel algorithm on inputs of size \(n\) has work \(T_1=\Theta(n^2)\) and span \(T_\infty=\Theta(n)\). We are interested in the time \(T_P\) used to run the algorithm on \(P\) processors with greedy scheduling. Which of the statements below are correct?

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Parallel algorithms (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: By CLRS Theorem 26.1, \(T_P \leq T_1 / P + T_\infty\), and by Theorem 26.2 this bound is within a factor 2 of the true running time. Substituting the given values of \(P\) yields: \[\begin{aligned} P=\Theta(1) &: \quad T_P=\Theta(n^2+n)=\Theta(n^2) \text{ which is } O(n^2),\\[4pt] P=\Theta(\log n) &: \quad T_P=\Theta\left(\frac{n^2}{\log n}+n\right) =\Theta\!\left(\frac{n^2}{\log n}\right)\text{ which is not } O(n\log n),\\[4pt] P=\Theta(n) &: \quad T_P=\Theta(n+n)=\Theta(n) \text{ which is } O(n),\\[4pt] P=\Theta(n^2/\log n) &: \quad T_P=\Theta(\log n+n)=\Theta(n) \text{ which is not } O(\log n),\\[4pt] P=\Theta(n^2) &: \quad T_P=\Theta(1+n)=\Theta(n) \text{ which is not } O(1). \end{aligned}\]

options.label: None of the above statements are always true.

data.stimulus:
Minimum spanning trees (4%)

Let \(G = (V,E)\) be a connected, simple graph with \(|V|=n\), and let \(w : E \to \mathbb{R}\) be an edge-weight function. Assume that all weights are distinct (i.e., that \(w\) is injective). Denote by \(M\) the number of distinct minimum spanning trees in \(G\) with respect to \(w\). Which of the following statements are always true, regardless of the choice of \(G\) and \(w\)?

Note that some of the statements are related in the sense that if one of them always holds, then the other one also always holds.

Select one or more correct answers.
data.title: Minimum spanning trees (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: There is always exactly one minimum spanning tree when all weights are distinct. If there were two different minimum spanning trees, one could consider the edge of minimum weight that appears in one tree but not in the other, and use the cut property to derive a contradiction. Therefore all of the inequalities are true except \(M \geq n\).

data.stimulus:
Balancing search trees (4%)

For an odd integer \(n\), let \(T\) be a highly unbalanced binary search tree with \(n\) keys and \((n+1)/2\) nodes on a path going to the right. Below is an illustration with \(n=9\) keys and a path of length 5.

What is the minimum number of rotations that must be performed to change \(T\) so that it has depth at most \(10 \log_2(n)\)? We are interested in the answer for large values of \(n\), expressed using asymptotic notation.

Exactly one answer is correct, but you may select more than one if you are in doubt.
data.title: Balancing search trees (4%)

metadata.distractor_rationale: Each rotation can reduce the depth by at most 1, so at least \(\Omega(n)\) rotations are required. We argue that \(O(n)\) rotations suffice: The rotations can be performed in iterations, where each iteration performs a left rotation at every second node on the path going to the right, e.g., 17 and 31 in the example. This reduces the length of the path by a factor of 2. After \(k\) iterations, every subtree hanging to the left of the right path has height at most \(k\). Therefore the depth of the tree becomes at most \(O(n/2^k + k)\). After \(k=\log_2(n)\) iterations the depth of the tree is at most \(2\log_2(n)\). The number of rotations in iteration \(k\) is \(\Theta(n/2^k)\), so the total number of rotations is \(\Theta(\sum_{k=1}^{\lg n} n/2^k)\), which is \(\Theta(n)\).

data.stimulus:
Interval covering (12%)

We are given a number \(L>0\) and a collection of \(n\) intervals \[I_i=[a_i,b_i],\] where \(i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\) and \(a_i < b_i\). We want to select as few intervals as possible such that their union covers the entire interval \([0,L]\). That is, we want to find \(J\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\) such that \([0,L]\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in J} I_i\) and \(\vert J\vert\) is as small as possible. The algorithm must return the size \(\vert J\vert\).

a)  Let \(L=12\), and let the intervals be \[[2,8],\ [-1,4],\ [1,5],\ [8,12],\ [6,20],\ [7,9].\] Give an optimal solution and briefly justify your answer.

metadata.sample_answer: An optimal solution is, e.g., \[[-1,4],\ [2,8],\ [6,20].\] (Another valid choice is \([-1,4]\), \([2,8]\), \([8,12]\)). These three intervals cover all of \([0,12]\). There is no solution with only two intervals: To cover \(0\) we must use \([-1,4]\), and no single interval covers all the way from \(4\) to \(12\). Therefore three intervals is optimal.

data.stimulus: b)  Describe an efficient algorithm that finds a minimum number of intervals covering \([0,L]\), if such a cover exists. If \([0,L]\) cannot be covered, the algorithm must return false. The input to the algorithm is \((a,b,n,L)\), where \(a[1{:}n]\) and \(b[1{:}n]\) are arrays of length \(n\) containing the start and end points, i.e., \(I_i=[a[i],b[i]]\). You may write pseudocode, but a clear and precise description in prose is also sufficient. You must account for the running time of the algorithm – to get full points it must be \(O(n\log n)\).

metadata.sample_answer:
First sort the intervals by left endpoint. We maintain a variable \(x\) indicating that we have already covered \([0,x]\). Initially \(x=0\). As long as \(x<L\), we scan all intervals that start at or before \(x\), and among these find the interval that reaches farthest to the right. If no such interval reaches beyond \(x\), then \([0,L]\) cannot be covered. Otherwise we select the interval and update \(x\). To scan the intervals efficiently, we maintain an index \(i\), so that we can start the search from the most recently added interval.

Sorting takes \(O(n\log n)\) time. After sorting, each interval is processed at most once in the inner while loop, so the rest of the algorithm takes \(O(n)\) time. The total running time is therefore \(O(n\log n)\).

data.stimulus: c)  Argue that the algorithm always finds a minimum number of intervals, if a cover exists.

metadata.sample_answer:
We show that the greedy choice is safe. Suppose that at some point the algorithm has covered the interval \([0,x]\). Any valid solution to the rest of the problem must use an interval \(I_i\) that starts at or before \(x\), since otherwise there would be a gap in the cover. Among all such intervals, the algorithm selects an interval \(I_{i^*}\) that reaches as far to the right as possible. If \(I_i\) and \(I_{i^*}\) are different intervals, we could replace \(I_i\) by \(I_{i^*}\) and still have a valid solution, since \(b[i^*]\geq b[i]\).

By induction on the number of intervals, it follows that the algorithm's choice in each step can be part of an optimal solution. The algorithm therefore finds the smallest possible number of intervals.

data.stimulus:
Increasing polygonal chain (12%)

We are given \(n\) points in the plane \(p_i=(x_i,y_i),\) where \(i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\). We assume that all \(x_i\)-coordinates are distinct.

An increasing polygonal chain is a sequence of points \[p_{i_1},p_{i_2},\ldots,p_{i_k}\] such that \[x_{i_1}<x_{i_2}<\cdots <x_{i_k} \text{ and } y_{i_1}<y_{i_2}<\cdots <y_{i_k} \enspace .\] Consider the problem of finding the length \(k\) of a longest possible increasing polygonal chain. Below is an example of a set of points and an increasing chain of length 3, illustrated as a path (not necessarily the longest).

a)  Consider the points shown in the figure above, i.e., \[\begin{array}{c|cccccccc} i & 1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\ \hline x_i & 1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\ y_i & 2&5&3&6&4&5&2&6 \end{array}\] Give a longest possible increasing polygonal chain.

metadata.sample_answer: A longest possible increasing polygonal chain is \[p_1,p_3,p_5,p_6,p_8.\] It has length \(5\) and is increasing, since \(2<3<4<5<6\) for the \(y\)-coordinates, and the points are already in increasing order of \(x\)-coordinate.

data.stimulus: b)  Describe an efficient algorithm that finds the length of a longest possible increasing polygonal chain. The input to the algorithm is arrays \(x[1{:}n]\) and \(y[1{:}n]\) of length \(n\), where point \(i\) is \((x[i],y[i])\). You must account for the running time of the algorithm – to get full points it must be \(O(n^2)\).

metadata.sample_answer:
First sort the points by increasing \(x\)-coordinate. Let \(D[i]\) be the length of a longest possible increasing chain ending at point \(i\). Then \[D[i] = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if there is no } j<i \text{ with } y[j]<y[i],\\ 1+\max\{D[j]\mid j<i \text{ and } y[j]<y[i]\}, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\]

Sorting takes \(O(n\log n)\) time. The two loops take \(O(n^2)\) time. The total running time is therefore \(O(n^2)\).

data.stimulus: c)  Argue that the algorithm always finds the length of a longest possible increasing polygonal chain.

metadata.sample_answer:
Consider a longest possible increasing chain ending at point \(i\). If the chain consists only of point \(i\), it has length \(1\). Otherwise the second-to-last point must be a point \(j\) with \(j<i\) and \(y[j]<y[i]\). The best chain ending at \(i\) is therefore obtained by taking the best chain ending at such a point \(j\) and appending point \(i\).

This is exactly what the recurrence for \(D[i]\) computes. Since the values \(D[j]\) for \(j<i\) have already been computed when \(D[i]\) is computed, correctness follows by induction on \(i\). Finally, an optimal chain can end at any point, so the algorithm returns \(\max_i D[i]\).
